final_proof:
For a map \(f:S_1\to S_2\), write \(f[U]=\{f(x):x\in U\}\). Saying that the restriction of the direct-image map to \(\tau_1\) is a surjection from \(\tau_1\) to \(\tau_2\) means both that \(f[U]\in\tau_2\) for every \(U\in\tau_1\), and that every member of \(\tau_2\) has this form. Thus condition (2) is equivalent to
\[
\tau_2=\{f[U]:U\in\tau_1\}. \tag{*}
\]

Suppose first that \((S_2,\tau_2)\) is a topological space homeomorphic to \(T_1=(S_1,\tau_1)\), and choose a homeomorphism \(f:S_1\to S_2\). By definition, \(f\) is a bijection, so (1) holds. Let \(g=f^{-1}:S_2\to S_1\) denote its inverse function. If \(U\in\tau_1\), then \(f[U]=g^{-1}[U]\), where the right-hand side is a preimage. Since \(g\) is continuous, \(f[U]\in\tau_2\). Hence the restricted direct-image map takes values in \(\tau_2\). Conversely, if \(V\in\tau_2\), continuity of \(f\) gives \(U=f^{-1}[V]\in\tau_1\), and surjectivity of \(f\) gives \(f[U]=f[f^{-1}[V]]=V\). Therefore the restricted direct-image map is onto \(\tau_2\), proving (2).

Conversely, suppose that a map \(f:S_1\to S_2\) satisfies (1) and (2). Then (*) holds. We first verify that \(\tau_2\) is a topology. Since \(\varnothing,S_1\in\tau_1\) and \(f\) is surjective,
\[
\varnothing=f[\varnothing]\in\tau_2,\qquad S_2=f[S_1]\in\tau_2.
\]
If \((V_i)_{i\in I}\) is any family in \(\tau_2\), then by (*) we may choose \(U_i\in\tau_1\) such that \(V_i=f[U_i]\). Direct images commute with arbitrary unions, so
\[
\bigcup_{i\in I}V_i=f\!\left[\bigcup_{i\in I}U_i\right]\in\tau_2.
\]
If \(V=f[U]\) and \(W=f[Z]\), where \(U,Z\in\tau_1\), injectivity of \(f\) yields
\[
V\cap W=f[U]\cap f[Z]=f[U\cap Z]\in\tau_2.
\]
Thus \(\tau_2\) contains the empty set and \(S_2\), is closed under arbitrary unions, and is closed under finite intersections; hence it is a topology on \(S_2\).

It remains to show that \(f\) is a homeomorphism. For each \(V\in\tau_2\), equation (*) supplies \(U\in\tau_1\) with \(V=f[U]\). Since \(f\) is injective,
\[
f^{-1}[V]=f^{-1}[f[U]]=U\in\tau_1,
\]
so \(f\) is continuous. Again let \(g=f^{-1}:S_2\to S_1\). For every \(U\in\tau_1\),
\[
g^{-1}[U]=f[U]\in\tau_2
\]
by (*), so \(g\) is continuous. Therefore \(f\) is a homeomorphism from \((S_1,\tau_1)\) to \((S_2,\tau_2)\). This proves both directions of the equivalence.
